title: Does FFmpeg keep my video's metadata?
fullTitle: FFmpeg Keeps Your Video's Location Tag by Default

scenes.narration: You edit a video with FFmpeg, and then you share it. Does the file still carry the title, the author, a comment, and the place where it was filmed? We build a test file with made-up tags, run four commands, and look inside the results two ways.

The source has five made-up tags: a title, an artist, a comment, a location in the open Atlantic, and a custom name on the video stream. We read each file two ways. ffprobe shows the tags. And we search the raw bytes of the file. The MP4 muxer stores a location as a binary atom called loci, so for that one we search for the atom's name.
captions: Title, artist, comment, location, handler name.
Two readers: ffprobe, and a raw byte search.

scenes.narration: A plain re-encode keeps all five. The title, the artist, the comment, the location, and the stream name. Both readers agree. Copying the streams with dash c copy keeps them as well.
Add dash map metadata minus one, and all five are gone. Both readers agree, with a re-encode and with dash c copy. That is the option for removing the tags.
One thing remains. The file still names the tool that wrote it: an encoder tag that starts with Lavf. Add dash fflags plus bitexact, and that tag is dropped from the format tags as well.
captions: Left behind: an encoder tag, Lavf.

scenes.narration: We tested only the tags we made. Real phone files carry more: location tracks, thumbnails, vendor specific atoms. We did not test them. If privacy matters, check the output yourself, with ffprobe and a byte search, before you share it.
captions: Not tested: real phone files, GPS tracks.
Check the output before you share it.

scenes.narration: Metadata survives by default, in re-encodes and in copies. Remove it on purpose. We saw the same results on ffmpeg six point one and eight point one. Not tested: real phone files, and other containers.
captions: Kept by default. Removed on purpose.
Not tested: real phone files, other containers.
